item.title: Enhancing Transparency and Replicability in Entrepreneurship Research with Preregistrations, Registered Reports, and Registered Revisions
item.content:encoded:
Katharina Fellnhofer, ETH Zurich

Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Thomas H. Allison, Texas Christian University

Pia Arenius, Emlyon Business School

Moren Lévesque, York University

J. Jeffrey Gish, Syracuse University

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice (ETP) is committed to working alongside entrepreneurship scholars to advance transparency, replicability, credibility, and rigor in empirical research. This special issue encourages authors to preregister research plans, submit empirical studies as Registered Reports — papers that receive editorial decisions before empirical results are known — and engage with ETP's contemporary Registered Revision process. ETP is pleased to announce a virtual special issue featuring Registered Reports, supporting its longstanding dedication to methodological innovation.

A growing body of literature spanning multiple disciplines including entrepreneurship explores the importance of credibility and replicability in scientific inquiry and how scientific rigor can be improved. This call for papers reinforces these efforts in entrepreneurship research by specifically advocating for scholars to submit studies as Registered Reports. The Registered Report format has evolved rapidly from a niche innovation to a widely adopted practice. Since the introduction of the Registered Report format in 2013, more than 300 journals have embraced the approach.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Replication and Robustness in Entrepreneurship Research
  • New Ways to Collect Data for Entrepreneurship
  • Importance of Null Results
  • Boundary Conditions, Mechanisms, Mediators, and Contextual Sensitivity
  • Longitudinal and Panel-Based Studies (Using Secondary Data)
  • Field Experiments and Entrepreneurial Interventions
  • Theory-Driven Exploratory Studies and Qualitative Studies
  • Meta-Science and Methods in Entrepreneurship Research

Timeline

  • December 22, 2026: Deadline for Registered Report submissions

item.title: Entrepreneurship Ex Machina: Transformative Artificial Intelligence for Theory and Practice
item.content:encoded:
Martin Obschonka, University of Amsterdam

Moren Lévesque, York University

Frédéric Ooms, HEC Liège

Jeffrey M. Pollack, NC State University

Denis A. Grégoire, HEC Montréal

Tara S. Behrend, Michigan State University

Boris Nikolaev, Colorado State University

Transformative Artificial Intelligence (AI) — that is, the use of AI tools that have such inherent capabilities that they could induce societal transitions similar to that of the agricultural or industrial revolutions — has become an omnipresent topic of interest. Because these tools offer order-of-magnitude efficiency improvements over prior ways of performing various human tasks, important research opportunities arise for better understanding their transformative impact.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Theorizing on algorithmic entrepreneurship
  • Mechanisms of external enablement of entrepreneurship via AI (e.g., generative AI)
  • Can AI help reduce the destructive aspects of entrepreneurship (e.g., societal and personal costs)?
  • Can AI create resource abundance, overcoming typical entrepreneurial resource scarcity and challenging leading startup methods (e.g., effectuation/bricolage, bootstrapping, lean startup)?
  • Do classic research findings and theories (e.g., on the role of knowledge and human and social capital in entrepreneurship) still hold in the new AI era?
  • How can AI impact entrepreneurial finance (e.g., AI-powered financial planning for entrepreneurs, VC investment portfolio management and decisions) and resource acquisition (e.g., entrepreneurs' pitch preparation, investors' due diligence, etc.)?
  • Does AI change the age curve associated with entrepreneurship (does it replace the advantage of industry experience, and do we therefore see an AI-empowered rise of youth entrepreneurs)?
  • How can AI contribute to equality and diversity (e.g., neurodiversity, closing the gender gap)?
  • Ethical and legal issues of algorithmic entrepreneurship and AI-supported research
  • How can AI support entrepreneurs' cognition, decision making, and psychological well-being?
  • Will the emerging AI economy of abundance replace entrepreneurship/human entrepreneurs?

Timeline

  • January 31, 2026: Final deadline for proposal submissions

item.title: Time in Entrepreneurship: New Perspectives and Approaches
item.content:encoded:
Ludvig Levasseur, Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

Moren Lévesque, York University

Paul Spee, University of Queensland

Ute Stephan, King's College London

Matthew Wood, University of Oklahoma

This special issue seeks manuscripts advancing our understanding of time in entrepreneurship. Research on the duration, pace, timing, and speed of action calibration in entrepreneurial processes such as opportunity realization are key examples of the role temporal dynamics play in entrepreneurship. Time is equally critical when examining decisions about the timing of growth while managing external events and shocks alongside slowly or rapidly evolving industry trends and customer preferences. Further lines of inquiry concern the pace, timing, and speed of exit decisions, or decisions to pursue venturing activities over time. Entrepreneurs' subjective perceptions of time, and their own and their stakeholders' orientations towards the short- vs. long-term, the past, present or future shape how they navigate entrepreneurship.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do objective dimensions such as duration, pace, timing, speed, and window of opportunity impact the entrepreneurship process?
  • How do they shape links between entrepreneurs' subjective time perspective, their biological time (chronotype), and cognitive processes related to information scanning and learning?
  • How do entrepreneurs' subjective time perspectives relate to their cognitions including information scanning and search, entrepreneurial learning, information associations and connections, and opportunity evaluation and judgment?
  • How do time perspectives relate to informal investors' and venture capitalists' decision to provide funding?
  • How do investors' time perspectives shape who they invest in, and the timing and size of their investments?
  • With what pace and speed do failure consequences vary with institutional and cultural contexts?
  • How does the timing of these consequences vary across groups of entrepreneurs including minoritized groups and differently abled entrepreneurs?
  • When and how does time perspective lead to unhealthy persistence in entrepreneurship and undermine well-being?
  • How do entrepreneurs' perception of time and the temporal development of the business impact venture emergence, business sustainability, and social entrepreneurship?
  • Do we see variations in temporal profiles and differences across industries and cultures?
  • How do the pacing of external events and entrepreneurs' own time perspective relate to how they manage equity, diversity, decolonization, and inclusion within their ventures?

Timeline

  • September 30, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Reexamining and Replicating Foundational Studies in Entrepreneurship Research
item.content:encoded:
Karl Wennberg, Stockholm School of Economics

Jeremy C. Short, University of North Texas

Jeffrey A. Chandler, University of North Texas

Marcus Wolfe, University of North Texas

Sebastian Kruse, RWTH University

Carolin Krieweth, RWTH University

This Special Issue seeks to advance our understanding of replication in entrepreneurship research by encouraging rigorous reexaminations of foundational empirical studies. Replication is essential for cumulative theory development and for establishing confidence in empirical findings. In a dynamic field such as entrepreneurship, where institutional environments, technologies, funding regimes, and societal expectations evolve rapidly, systematic replication is particularly critical to assess whether foundational relationships reflect stable theoretical mechanisms or context-specific patterns.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • The 33 most cited entrepreneurship studies (each exceeding 1,000 citations) identified as priority candidates for replication
  • Influential studies within specific BCERC research tracks highlighted as influential contributions within each track
  • Studies with credible cases for broader influence on entrepreneurship research
  • Identifying boundary conditions and contextual contingencies of established relationships
  • Clarifying inconsistencies or mixed findings in prior research
  • Refining theoretical mechanisms underlying key constructs and relationships
  • Contributing to methodological transparency, rigor, and best practices in replication research
  • Multi-study designs combining exact replication or reanalysis of original data with subsequent empirical generalization or theoretical extension

Timeline

  • December 1, 2026: Deadline for short proposal submission for paper development workshop participation (3,000-5,000 words)
  • February 1, 2027: In-person paper development workshop at University of North Texas
  • March 1, 2027: Virtual paper development workshop

  • August 1, 2027: Manuscript submission deadline (midnight U.S. Eastern Time)

item.title: The Startup Workforce
item.content:encoded:
James Bort, DePaul University

Veroniek Collewaert, Vlerick Business School

Yuval Engel, University of Amsterdam

Evy Van Lancker, Ghent University

Johan Wiklund, Syracuse University

The startup workforce represents a distinct and consequential stakeholder in entrepreneurship that has been systematically understudied relative to founders and funders. Early insights from the Stanford Project on Emerging Companies revealed how organizational changes within startups disproportionately impacted long-tenured employees. This pioneering work laid the foundation for understanding how startups differ from established firms in their approach to human capital, including fundamental aspects such as compensation, staffing, and performance management.

Contemporary research has deepened our understanding of the unique dynamics between startups and their employees. Whereas early research identified demographic patterns, illustrating that startup employees tend to be younger and risk-tolerant, recent work has uncovered more nuanced dynamics. For example, experienced employees often join startups when they have partners with stable careers, but can also command wage premiums as firms grow. Startup employees are drawn in by passionate founders, opportunities for greater freedom and responsibility, and the potential for significant financial upside.

Appel publié par Entrepreneurship Theory and Practice. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Employee motivations and retention across venture stages
  • Recruitment, employer branding, and the role of prior affiliations in startup hiring
  • The influence of early employees on organizational culture, routines, and strategic direction
  • Compensation structures, equity arrangements, and evolving psychological contracts
  • Workforce well-being, occupational stress, and founder-employee emotional spillovers
  • The impact of hybrid and remote work on startup employment dynamics
  • The opportunities and adversity of AI in light of startup employment and work ethic, and workforce diversity, inclusion, and the role of HR professionalization in early-stage ventures
  • Worker voice, collective action, and power asymmetries in startups, including unionization, whistleblowing, hustle culture and exploitation, equity and vesting disputes, and the dark side of founder–employee relations
  • The regulatory and institutional environment of startup employment, including non-compete enforcement, worker classification, equity taxation, and visa regimes
  • Non-standard and hybrid labor forms, including contractors, fractional executives, agencies, platform and ghost work, and globally distributed teams
  • Post-startup career trajectories, including employee mobility, alumni networks, and entrepreneurial spawning after exit, acquisition, or failure
  • The scaleup transition and its workforce implications, including when and how a startup workforce ceases to be one and how HR professionalization reshapes the employment relation
  • AI-native ventures as a new organizational form, where a small number of humans operate agentic systems and the category of workforce is itself reconstituted
  • Startup workforces outside North America and Western Europe, including emerging-economy, informal, and cross-border contexts

Timeline

  • May 1, 2027: Special issue editorial workshop for invited participants based on proposals (hosted in United States)
  • August 30, 2027: Full papers due for submission following second workshop
